The evolution from legacy to smart grid interface devices represents a fundamental shift in how buildings can inter- act with the electrical grid and other utilities. Legacy devices create a barrier between building operations and grid conditions, while smart devices enable buildings to become active participants in grid management through demand response, peak shaving, and distributed energy resource coordination. However, the integration of these smart de- vices with existing building control systems often requires careful planning to ensure compatibility and realize the full potential of enhanced grid-building interactions. 7 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications 2.2 Grid Devices The electrical grid presents a complex landscape of aging infrastructure that spans multiple decades of technological development. Workshop participants identified a comprehensive inventory of legacy equipment currently deployed across grid operations, revealing the diverse ecosystem of devices that must interoperate despite varying ages, capa- bilities, and communication protocols. These devices can be categorized based on their primary functions within the grid infrastructure. 2.2.1 Generation and Power Conversion Equipment Legacy generation and power conversion equipment forms the backbone of electricity production and conditioning across the grid. • Power Plant Controllersmanage the operation of conventional generators, controlling startup sequences, load dispatch, and safety systems. Older controllers often rely on proprietary protocols and may lack integration capabilities with modern grid management systems. The transition to more flexible, responsive generation requires upgrading these controllers to support faster response times and better communication with grid operators. • Conventional Generatorsinclude older coal, natural gas, and nuclear plants that were designed for baseload operation rather than the flexible, responsive generation needed in modern grids. These legacy generators often have longer startup times, minimum operating levels, and limited ramping capabilities compared to newer, more flexible generation resources (DOE OE 2021). • Photovoltaics (PV) Invertersrepresent a rapidly evolving technology where equipment quickly becomes outdated. Older photovoltaic inverters may lack advanced grid support functions such as voltage regulation, frequency response, and ride-through capabilities during grid disturbances. They often cannot participate in grid services that newer smart inverters can provide, limiting their contribution to grid stability and resilience. • Power System Stabilizersare control systems for synchronous generation that help maintain grid stability. Legacy stabilizers may use outdated control algorithms and lack the sophisticated coordination capabilities needed for modern grid operations with distributed resources and varying load patterns. As renewable energy and distributed generation reshape electricity production, upgrading these legacy controllers and generators becomes important not just for improved performance, but to enable the flexible, responsive genera- tion capabilities that modern grids fundamentally require. 2.2.2 Transmission and Distribution Infrastructure The physical infrastructure for power delivery faces a dual challenge: expanding access to remote and rural areas while simultaneously modernizing decades-old equipment across both sparsely and densely populated regions (DOE GDO 2023).
